title: Units, Vectors, and Mathematical Reasoning

sections.overview: Every MCAT physics question ultimately reduces to math — units, vectors, and mathematical reasoning are the language through which all physical relationships are expressed. The MCAT tests your ability to work fluently in this language under time pressure: converting between unit prefixes, using dimensional analysis to catch errors or derive formulas, decomposing vectors into components, interpreting slopes and areas on graphs, and using proportional reasoning to predict how changing one variable affects another without full calculation. These are not isolated skills — they weave through every physics topic on the exam. A kinematics question might require vector decomposition of initial velocity; a fluids passage may ask you to infer a relationship from a graph; an electrostatics problem may test your ability to reason proportionally about Coulomb's law. sections.collegeNotes:
## SI Units

The International System of Units (SI) defines seven base units from which all other units are derived. For the MCAT, the essential base units are: meter (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, ampere (A) for electric current, kelvin (K) for temperature, mole (mol) for amount of substance, and candela (cd) for luminous intensity (rarely tested). All other MCAT-relevant units are derived: force is the newton (N = kg·m/s²), energy and work are the joule (J = N·m = kg·m²/s²), power is the watt (W = J/s = kg·m²/s³), pressure is the pascal (Pa = N/m² = kg/m·s²), electric potential is the volt (V = J/C = kg·m²/A·s³), and frequency is the hertz (Hz = s⁻¹). The MCAT also tests metric prefixes comprehensively: know tera- (T, 10¹²), giga- (G, 10⁹), mega- (M, 10⁶), kilo- (k, 10³), centi- (c, 10⁻²), milli- (m, 10⁻³), micro- (μ, 10⁻⁶), nano- (n, 10⁻⁹), and pico- (p, 10⁻¹²). A critical exam skill is converting between units using dimensional analysis — e.g., converting 5 mm² to m² requires squaring the conversion factor: 5 mm² × (10⁻³ m/mm)² = 5 × 10⁻⁶ m². Pay special attention to squared and cubed unit conversions, as these are common error sources.

## Dimensional Analysis

Dimensional analysis treats units as algebraic quantities that must balance on both sides of an equation. This technique serves two vital functions on the MCAT: (1) error detection — if the units on the left side do not match the units on the right side, the equation is wrong; and (2) formula reconstruction — if you can identify the relevant variables and their units, you can often deduce the correct relationship. The process: write the units of each variable, combine them according to the operation in the formula, and verify the result matches the expected units of the quantity being calculated. Example: Pressure is force per unit area. Force has units of N = kg·m/s². Area has units of m². Therefore pressure must have units of (kg·m/s²)/m² = kg/m·s² = Pa. The MCAT frequently asks: 'Which of the following expressions has units of...?' — dimensional analysis solves these quickly. For literal equations with unknown exponents, you can set up: [Quantity] = [variable1]^a × [variable2]^b, substitute the units, and solve for a and b by requiring the exponents of each base unit (kg, m, s) to match. Dimensional analysis cannot determine dimensionless constants (e.g., 1/2, pi, sqrt(2)) but these are rarely tested on the MCAT. Trigonometric functions, exponentials, and logarithms are dimensionless — their arguments must also be dimensionless.

## Scientific Notation

Scientific notation expresses numbers as a coefficient (between 1 and 10) multiplied by a power of ten: a × 10^n. The MCAT requires rapid manipulation of scientific notation without a calculator. Key operations: multiplication adds exponents ((a×10^n)(b×10^m) = (ab)×10^(n+m)), division subtracts exponents ((a×10^n)/(b×10^m) = (a/b)×10^(n-m)), powers multiply the exponent ((a×10^n)^k = a^k×10^(nk)), and roots divide the exponent (sqrt(a×10^n) = sqrt(a)×10^(n/2) — adjust so n is even first). For addition and subtraction, convert to the same exponent first. Example: 3.2×10^4 + 5.1×10^3 = 3.2×10^4 + 0.51×10^4 = 3.71×10^4. Significant figures matter for MCAT passages but are rarely the primary testing point: multiplication/division keeps the fewest sig figs of any factor; addition/subtraction keeps the fewest decimal places. A common MCAT shortcut: when answer choices differ by orders of magnitude, you can often estimate the exponent without computing the coefficient precisely.

## Vector Components

Vectors are quantities with both magnitude and direction — the MCAT tests vectors primarily through forces, velocities, accelerations, momenta, and fields. Scalar quantities (mass, time, temperature, energy, speed) have magnitude only. Vector addition follows the head-to-tail rule: place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first; the resultant runs from the tail of the first to the head of the last. The core skill is resolving a vector into perpendicular components (almost always x and y). Given a vector of magnitude A at angle theta from the horizontal: Ax = A cos theta, Ay = A sin theta. Reconstruct magnitude: A = sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2). Direction: theta = tan^-1(Ay/Ax), with quadrant adjustments (if Ax < 0, add or subtract 180 degrees as appropriate). For vector addition by components: Rx = Ax + Bx, Ry = Ay + By, then compute R and theta_R. Vector subtraction: A - B = A + (-B), where -B has the same magnitude as B but the opposite direction. For the MCAT, the most common angles are 0, 30, 45, 60, and 90 degrees. Memorize sin values: sin 30 = 1/2, sin 45 = sqrt(2)/2 = 0.707, sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2 = 0.866; cos follows the reverse. Dot product (A dot B = AB cos theta) yields a scalar representing parallel projection; cross product magnitude (|A x B| = AB sin theta) yields a vector perpendicular to both — used in torque and magnetic force.

## Trigonometry

Right-triangle trigonometry is essential for vector resolution and for analyzing inclined planes, pendulums, and forces at angles. The three primary ratios: sine = opposite/hypotenuse, cosine = adjacent/hypotenuse, tangent = opposite/adjacent. The MCAT primarily uses these to find components of a vector or to find an angle from components. Key exact values to memorize: sin 0 = 0, sin 30 = 0.5, sin 45 = sqrt(2)/2 = 0.71, sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2 = 0.87, sin 90 = 1; cos follows the reverse (cos 0 = 1, cos 90 = 0). For small angles (theta < ~15 degrees or ~0.25 rad), the small-angle approximation is extremely useful: sin theta = theta (in radians), tan theta = theta, cos theta = 1 - theta^2/2 = 1. This appears in pendulum problems and single-slit diffraction. The Pythagorean theorem (a^2 + b^2 = c^2) is used constantly to find resultant vector magnitudes. Know the common Pythagorean triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, and recognize scaled versions like 6-8-10. The inverse trig functions (arcsin, arccos, arctan) are rarely computed exactly on the MCAT; you will typically compare which angle is larger by reasoning about the ratio. Radian measure: pi radians = 180 degrees. Common conversions: 90 = pi/2, 60 = pi/3, 45 = pi/4, 30 = pi/6. Angular measurements and small-angle approximations require radian mode.

## Graph Interpretation

The MCAT frequently presents experimental data as graphs and asks you to extract relationships, slopes, areas, and intercepts. Linear graphs (y = mx + b): slope m is the rate of change; the y-intercept b is the value when x = 0. The MCAT tests whether you can identify what physical quantity the slope represents — for example, on a velocity-time graph the slope is acceleration and the area under the curve is displacement. Always check axis labels and units before interpreting. Nonlinear graphs: inverse relationships (y proportional to 1/x) produce hyperbolas — as x increases, y decreases but never reaches zero. Square relationships (y proportional to x^2) produce parabolas. Inverse-square relationships (y proportional to 1/x^2) drop off more steeply than simple inverse. For passage-based questions, the most common task is reasoning about how changing one variable affects another at a specific point on the curve (proportional reasoning) or extrapolating beyond the plotted range. Straight-line graphs from nonlinear data: if you suspect y proportional to x^2, plot y vs. x^2 and check for linearity; if you suspect y proportional to 1/x, plot y vs. 1/x and check for linearity. This linearization strategy is a classic passage-analysis skill. Log-log and semi-log plots appear occasionally; on a log-log plot, a power-law relationship appears as a straight line whose slope equals the exponent. Area under the curve: for linear graphs, area = 1/2(base)(height) for triangles plus base times height for rectangles. The physical meaning of the area depends on the axes: area under a Force-displacement graph = work; area under a Pressure-volume graph = work; area under a current-time graph = charge.

## Proportional Reasoning

Proportional reasoning is arguably the highest-yield mathematical skill on the MCAT — it allows you to answer quantitative questions without full calculation by analyzing how a quantity changes when one or more variables change while others are held constant. The method: (1) Write the governing equation; (2) Identify which variables change and which are constant; (3) Express the relationship as a proportion: Q is proportional to [variable expression]; (4) Plug in the factor by which each variable changes; (5) Compute the net factor. Example: The period of a pendulum is T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g). If length L is quadrupled (x4), then T is proportional to sqrt(L) so T increases by sqrt(4) = 2x. If gravitational acceleration g were instead increased by a factor of 4, T would decrease by sqrt(1/4) = 1/2. Common proportional relationships on the MCAT: F_gravity proportional to 1/r^2 (inverse square); F_spring proportional to x (Hooke's law, direct); P proportional to 1/V (Boyle's law, inverse); v_wave proportional to sqrt(T/mu) (wave speed on a string); R proportional to L/A (resistance). A key distinction: direct proportion (y = kx, linear through origin) vs. linear relationship (y = mx + b, line not necessarily through origin). Only directly proportional quantities have a constant ratio y/x = k. For combined proportionality: if y is proportional to a^2 * b / sqrt(c), and a doubles, b triples, and c quadruples, then y changes by (2^2)(3)/sqrt(4) = (4)(3)/2 = 6 — so y increases by a factor of 6. Practice mental estimation: when c doubles, sqrt(c) increases by ~1.4, so y decreases by a factor of ~0.71.

## How it works

MCAT mathematical reasoning is a unified toolchain. Start with SI units as the vocabulary — every quantity has a unit signature. Use dimensional analysis as a grammar check: if the units don't balance, the equation cannot be right. Scientific notation lets you handle the enormous range of scales from subatomic (10^-15 m) to astronomical (10^9 m) without losing track of zeros. When quantities have direction, represent them as vectors and decompose into perpendicular components using trigonometry (SOHCAHTOA). Once components are isolated, they behave independently — horizontal motion does not affect vertical motion. For passage-based questions, graphs encode relationships visually: slopes give rates, areas give accumulations, and the curve shape reveals the proportionality (linear, inverse, square, inverse-square). Proportional reasoning is the synthesis skill — given a formula and a scenario where one variable changes, you can predict the effect on the result without computing absolute values. Together, these tools let you move fluidly between physical intuition and mathematical precision, which is exactly what the MCAT Chemical and Physical Foundations section demands.

sections.comparisons:
- C/P (Kinematics PH-002): Vector decomposition of initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components is essential for projectile motion; proportional reasoning applied to constant-acceleration equations.
- C/P (Forces PH-003): Free-body diagrams require resolving forces (gravity on inclines, tension at angles) into components; trigonometric functions determine the component magnitudes.
- C/P (Fluids PH-007): Dimensional analysis verifies pressure (Pa = N/m^2) and flow rate (m^3/s); proportional reasoning with Poiseuille's law (Q proportional to r^4) — a 2x radius increase yields 16x flow.
- C/P (Electrostatics PH-009): Coulomb's law (F proportional to 1/r^2) and electric field (E proportional to 1/r^2) are classic inverse-square proportional reasoning targets; vector addition for superposition of forces.
- C/P (Circuits PH-010): Ohm's law (V = IR) tested via graph interpretation (V vs. I slope = R); proportional reasoning for series vs. parallel resistance.
- C/P (Waves PH-011): Wave equation (v = f*lambda) tested via proportional reasoning — if frequency doubles and speed is constant, wavelength halves; graph interpretation of displacement vs. time and displacement vs. position.
- B/B (Physiology): Graph interpretation for pressure-volume loops (cardiac), flow-volume curves (pulmonary), and dose-response curves (pharmacology); proportional reasoning for Fick's law and Hagen-Poiseuille flow.
sections.commonConfusions:
- Squaring unit conversion factors incorrectly. Converting 5 cm^2 to m^2: it is 5 x (10^-2)^2 = 5 x 10^-4 m^2, NOT 5 x 10^-2 m^2. Area and volume conversions are the most common unit errors on the MCAT.
- Using sine instead of cosine (or vice versa) for vector components. Sine gives the component opposite the angle; cosine gives the component adjacent to the angle. On inclined planes, always redraw the triangle and confirm which side you need.
- Forgetting that trigonometric functions are dimensionless. When doing dimensional analysis, sin theta, cos theta, and e^x contribute no units — treat them as dimensionless coefficients.
- Confusing slope and area under the curve. On a velocity-time graph, slope = acceleration, but area = displacement. The MCAT will offer both as answer choices to trap students who mix them up.
- Assuming a linear relationship when the equation is not directly proportional. y = mx + b is linear but NOT directly proportional unless b = 0. Direct proportionality requires a zero y-intercept and constant ratio y/x.
- Treating vectors as scalars. Adding two 5 N forces can yield anything from 0 N (opposite directions) to 10 N (same direction). Always consider direction when working with vectors.
- Using degrees in formulas that require radians. Angular velocity, small-angle approximations, and arc-length formulas (s = r*theta) all require radians. Convert: theta_rad = theta_deg * pi/180.
- Mishandling inverse-square reasoning. If distance triples, force decreases by 1/3^2 = 1/9, NOT 1/3. The square is on the distance, not on the force factor.
sections.eli10: Think of physics math as a universal translator. SI units are the dictionary — every measurement has a word (meter, kilogram, second) and those words combine to form sentences (N = kg*m/s^2). Dimensional analysis is the grammar checker — if the sentence doesn't follow the rules, it's nonsense, and you can catch mistakes without understanding the full meaning. Scientific notation is shorthand — instead of writing out a googol of zeros, you write x10^n and keep your paper clean. Vectors are arrows that point somewhere — when an arrow points diagonally, trigonometry splits it into a horizontal piece and a vertical piece, like breaking a diagonal move on a chessboard into a sideways step and a forward step. Those two pieces don't interfere with each other — you solve horizontal and vertical problems independently. Graphs are picture translations of relationships: a straight line means 'this and that change together at a steady rate,' a curve that flattens means 'the effect gets weaker as you go.' Proportional reasoning is the ultimate shortcut — instead of doing the full math, you ask: 'If I double this, what happens to that?' That one question, applied to the right equation, answers most MCAT physics problems in seconds. The limitation: these tools tell you how quantities relate, but not why. Proportional reasoning can tell you that gravity weakens with the square of distance, but it cannot tell you why nature chose an inverse-square law over something else.
sections.quickReview:
- SI base units: meter (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol). Derived: N = kg*m/s^2, J = N*m, W = J/s, Pa = N/m^2, V = J/C, Hz = s^-1.
- Metric prefixes: T(12), G(9), M(6), k(3), c(-2), m(-3), u(-6), n(-9), p(-12). Area conversions square the factor; volume conversions cube it.
- Dimensional analysis: treat units algebraically. Both sides must match. Cannot determine dimensionless constants (1/2, pi). Trig/log/exp functions are dimensionless.
- Vector components: Ax = A cos(theta), Ay = A sin(theta). Magnitude: A = sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2). Direction: theta = tan^-1(Ay/Ax) with quadrant check.
- Vector addition: Rx = Ax + Bx, Ry = Ay + By. Subtraction: A - B = A + (-B). Dot: A*B = AB cos(theta) (scalar). Cross: |AxB| = AB sin(theta) (vector).
- Trig values: sin 30 = 1/2, sin 45 = sqrt(2)/2, sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2. cos mirrors. tan = sin/cos.
- Small-angle approx (theta in rad): sin(theta) = theta, tan(theta) = theta, cos(theta) = 1. Radians: pi rad = 180 deg. Convert: theta_rad = theta_deg * pi/180.
- Graphs: slope = delta-y/delta-x = rate; area under curve = accumulation. On v-t graph: slope = a, area = delta-x. Linearization: plot y vs. x^n to test y proportional to x^n.
- Proportional reasoning: y ~ x => double x, double y. y ~ x^2 => double x, quadruple y. y ~ 1/x => double x, halve y. y ~ 1/x^2 => double x, quarter y.
- Direct proportion (y = kx) vs. linear (y = mx + b): only direct proportion has constant y/x and passes through origin.
- Sci notation: multiply = add exponents; divide = subtract; power = multiply exponent; root = divide exponent (make n even first).
- Common triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 6-8-10. Pythagorean: c^2 = a^2 + b^2. Use for resultant vectors.

MCAT mathematical reasoning is a unified toolchain. Start with SI units as the vocabulary — every quantity has a unit signature. Use dimensional analysis as a grammar check: if the units don't balance, the equation cannot be right. Scientific notation lets you handle the enormous range of scales from subatomic (10^-15 m) to astronomical (10^9 m) without losing track of zeros. When quantities have direction, represent them as vectors and decompose into perpendicular components using trigonometry (SOHCAHTOA). Once components are isolated, they behave independently — horizontal motion does not affect vertical motion. For passage-based questions, graphs encode relationships visually: slopes give rates, areas give accumulations, and the curve shape reveals the proportionality (linear, inverse, square, inverse-square). Proportional reasoning is the synthesis skill — given a formula and a scenario where one variable changes, you can predict the effect on the result without computing absolute values. Together, these tools let you move fluidly between physical intuition and mathematical precision, which is exactly what the MCAT Chemical and Physical Foundations section demands.

## MCAT Connections
- C/P (Kinematics PH-002): Vector decomposition of initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components is essential for projectile motion; proportional reasoning applied to constant-acceleration equations.
- C/P (Forces PH-003): Free-body diagrams require resolving forces (gravity on inclines, tension at angles) into components; trigonometric functions determine the component magnitudes.
- C/P (Fluids PH-007): Dimensional analysis verifies pressure (Pa = N/m^2) and flow rate (m^3/s); proportional reasoning with Poiseuille's law (Q proportional to r^4) — a 2x radius increase yields 16x flow.
- C/P (Electrostatics PH-009): Coulomb's law (F proportional to 1/r^2) and electric field (E proportional to 1/r^2) are classic inverse-square proportional reasoning targets; vector addition for superposition of forces.
- C/P (Circuits PH-010): Ohm's law (V = IR) tested via graph interpretation (V vs. I slope = R); proportional reasoning for series vs. parallel resistance.
- C/P (Waves PH-011): Wave equation (v = f*lambda) tested via proportional reasoning — if frequency doubles and speed is constant, wavelength halves; graph interpretation of displacement vs. time and displacement vs. position.
- B/B (Physiology): Graph interpretation for pressure-volume loops (cardiac), flow-volume curves (pulmonary), and dose-response curves (pharmacology); proportional reasoning for Fick's law and Hagen-Poiseuille flow.

## High-Yield MCAT Traps

1. Squaring unit conversion factors incorrectly. Converting 5 cm^2 to m^2: it is 5 x (10^-2)^2 = 5 x 10^-4 m^2, NOT 5 x 10^-2 m^2. Area and volume conversions are the most common unit errors on the MCAT.

2. Using sine instead of cosine (or vice versa) for vector components. Sine gives the component opposite the angle; cosine gives the component adjacent to the angle. On inclined planes, always redraw the triangle and confirm which side you need.

3. Forgetting that trigonometric functions are dimensionless. When doing dimensional analysis, sin theta, cos theta, and e^x contribute no units — treat them as dimensionless coefficients.

4. Confusing slope and area under the curve. On a velocity-time graph, slope = acceleration, but area = displacement. The MCAT will offer both as answer choices to trap students who mix them up.

5. Assuming a linear relationship when the equation is not directly proportional. y = mx + b is linear but NOT directly proportional unless b = 0. Direct proportionality requires a zero y-intercept and constant ratio y/x.

6. Treating vectors as scalars. Adding two 5 N forces can yield anything from 0 N (opposite directions) to 10 N (same direction). Always consider direction when working with vectors.

7. Using degrees in formulas that require radians. Angular velocity, small-angle approximations, and arc-length formulas (s = r*theta) all require radians. Convert: theta_rad = theta_deg * pi/180.

8. Mishandling inverse-square reasoning. If distance triples, force decreases by 1/3^2 = 1/9, NOT 1/3. The square is on the distance, not on the force factor.

## ELI-10 Explains
Think of physics math as a universal translator. SI units are the dictionary — every measurement has a word (meter, kilogram, second) and those words combine to form sentences (N = kg*m/s^2). Dimensional analysis is the grammar checker — if the sentence doesn't follow the rules, it's nonsense, and you can catch mistakes without understanding the full meaning. Scientific notation is shorthand — instead of writing out a googol of zeros, you write x10^n and keep your paper clean. Vectors are arrows that point somewhere — when an arrow points diagonally, trigonometry splits it into a horizontal piece and a vertical piece, like breaking a diagonal move on a chessboard into a sideways step and a forward step. Those two pieces don't interfere with each other — you solve horizontal and vertical problems independently. Graphs are picture translations of relationships: a straight line means 'this and that change together at a steady rate,' a curve that flattens means 'the effect gets weaker as you go.' Proportional reasoning is the ultimate shortcut — instead of doing the full math, you ask: 'If I double this, what happens to that?' That one question, applied to the right equation, answers most MCAT physics problems in seconds. The limitation: these tools tell you how quantities relate, but not why. Proportional reasoning can tell you that gravity weakens with the square of distance, but it cannot tell you why nature chose an inverse-square law over something else.

## Quick Recall
1. SI base units: meter (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol). Derived: N = kg*m/s^2, J = N*m, W = J/s, Pa = N/m^2, V = J/C, Hz = s^-1.
2. Metric prefixes: T(12), G(9), M(6), k(3), c(-2), m(-3), u(-6), n(-9), p(-12). Area conversions square the factor; volume conversions cube it.
3. Dimensional analysis: treat units algebraically. Both sides must match. Cannot determine dimensionless constants (1/2, pi). Trig/log/exp functions are dimensionless.
4. Vector components: Ax = A cos(theta), Ay = A sin(theta). Magnitude: A = sqrt(Ax^2 + Ay^2). Direction: theta = tan^-1(Ay/Ax) with quadrant check.
5. Vector addition: Rx = Ax + Bx, Ry = Ay + By. Subtraction: A - B = A + (-B). Dot: A*B = AB cos(theta) (scalar). Cross: |AxB| = AB sin(theta) (vector).
6. Trig values: sin 30 = 1/2, sin 45 = sqrt(2)/2, sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2. cos mirrors. tan = sin/cos.
7. Small-angle approx (theta in rad): sin(theta) = theta, tan(theta) = theta, cos(theta) = 1. Radians: pi rad = 180 deg. Convert: theta_rad = theta_deg * pi/180.
8. Graphs: slope = delta-y/delta-x = rate; area under curve = accumulation. On v-t graph: slope = a, area = delta-x. Linearization: plot y vs. x^n to test y proportional to x^n.
9. Proportional reasoning: y ~ x => double x, double y. y ~ x^2 => double x, quadruple y. y ~ 1/x => double x, halve y. y ~ 1/x^2 => double x, quarter y.
10. Direct proportion (y = kx) vs. linear (y = mx + b): only direct proportion has constant y/x and passes through origin.
11. Sci notation: multiply = add exponents; divide = subtract; power = multiply exponent; root = divide exponent (make n even first).
12. Common triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 6-8-10. Pythagorean: c^2 = a^2 + b^2. Use for resultant vectors.
